insider_note: A power of cosx multiplied by a bare sinx is always the t=cosx trigger — the lone sinx supplies exactly the −dt the substitution needs.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Substitute t = cosx
lines: Put cosx = t ⇒ −sinx dx = dt, i.e. sinx dx = −dt
steps.why: cos³x sinx dx is exactly t³ times −dt once t=cosx, since the lone sinx factor is precisely (minus) the derivative of cosx.
common_mistakes: Missing the minus sign that comes from d/dx(cosx)=−sinx, and writing +dt instead of −dt.
Trying t=sinx instead, which does not match the lone sinx factor needed for dt.
steps.memory_tip: A power of cosx TIMES sinx ⇒ t=cosx, dt=−sinx dx — the minus sign always comes along for the ride.

steps.label: Integrate and back-substitute for the final answer
steps.why: −∫t³dt = −t⁴/4 + c by the power rule, and substituting t=cosx back in gives the final answer as a negative quarter power of cos⁴x.
common_mistakes: Losing the leading minus sign, writing +cos⁴x/4 instead.
Forgetting to substitute cosx back in for t.
steps.memory_tip: The minus sign picked up at the substitution step survives all the way to the final boxed answer.
